hero.lede: Portrait on Gold sells personalised, made-to-order gold portraits. I built and customised its Shopify storefront: custom product-option logic, app-free filtering, a responsive mobile experience and a WhatsApp check on cash-on-delivery orders before production.

facts: Full Stack Developer (Diviniti & Portrait on Gold)

sections.title: Overview
sections.lead: A made-to-order store where every product is personal, so every unconfirmed order has a real cost.
paras: Customers choose a collection and a form for their portrait, and the store produces it to order. I built the product-option logic, the collection filtering and a WhatsApp-first order check, and optimised the storefront for mobile shoppers.

sections.title: The Challenge
items: Personalised options. The collection and form choices had to be clear on the product page.
Filtering without another app. Collections needed filtering, but the store was avoiding paid Shopify apps.
Fake COD orders. Unconfirmed cash-on-delivery orders are a common problem for personalised products in India. Here, each one meant a portrait produced for nobody.

sections.title: Constraints
items: No paid filter or variant apps. The store had to stay lean, without recurring subscriptions.
Verification had to happen before production, not after a failed delivery, because a personalised portrait can't be resold.
Most traffic for personalised gifting arrives from mobile ad clicks, so every flow had to work well on a phone.

sections.title: My Role
paras: I wrote the collection filtering in JavaScript, the product-option logic in Liquid and the WhatsApp verification flow through WATI, and tuned the storefront layout for mobile.

sections.title: What I Built
items: Custom Liquid product-option logic for the collection and form choices, with metafield-driven product content.
App-free collection filtering in JavaScript, in place of a paid filter app.
A WhatsApp-first COD verification flow through WATI, so orders are confirmed before fulfilment.
A responsive, mobile-first storefront for shoppers arriving from ads.

sections.title: Key Improvements
steps: Order placed
A customer places a cash-on-delivery order for a personalised portrait.
WhatsApp confirmation
The order is followed up on WhatsApp through WATI, asking the customer to confirm.
Confirmed before production
The team only produces confirmed orders. Unconfirmed ones are caught before any material or time is spent.

sections.title: The Hard Part
paras: Why custom code instead of another app? A filter app would have added a monthly fee and more third-party script to every collection page, on a store where most visitors arrive on mobile. Filtering in JavaScript against data the theme already outputs kept collection pages lean and under the store's control.

The verification step wasn't something a theme app could solve either. It has to connect an order to a WhatsApp conversation and a human decision before fulfilment, which makes it an integration problem (WATI wired into the order flow), not a storefront setting.

code.note: Simplified sketch of the filtering approach, not the production code
code.html: {%- comment -%} Each product card carries its filterable values {%- endcomment -%} <li data-product-card data-form="{{ product.options_by_name['Form'].values | join: ',' }}"> // Filter in the browser: no app, no page reload const cards = [...document.querySelectorAll('[data-product-card]')]; function applyFilters(active) { // e.g. { form: 'Round' } cards.forEach(card => { card.hidden = !Object.entries(active).every(([key, value]) => !value || card.dataset[key].split(',').includes(value)); }); }

sections.title: Results
items: Collection and form chosen on the product page, handled by Liquid logic.
No paid filter app. Collections filter with custom JavaScript.
Cash-on-delivery orders confirmed on WhatsApp before a personalised portrait goes into production.

pog.takeaway: The most valuable change wasn't on the storefront. It was putting a verification step in the right place in the order flow. Custom code made sense where an app would have added cost or couldn't reach the problem.

glance.problem: Every portrait is made to order, so an unconfirmed cash-on-delivery order means a portrait produced for nobody.
glance.contribution: I built custom product-option logic in Liquid and added WhatsApp confirmation for cash-on-delivery orders through WATI.
glance.outcome: Cash-on-delivery orders are confirmed before production, and shoppers choose a collection and a form on the product page.

metrics.label: Schema-driven Liquid sections the team edits without code

sections.title: Overview
sections.lead: A luxury catalogue where page speed and merchandising flexibility both mattered.
paras: The work covered the Shopify theme end to end: how images load, how pages are built and edited, and how customer behaviour is measured. Across the 500+ products I managed, any inefficiency in one image or section repeats across every collection and product page, so the fixes had to be systemic.

sections.title: The Challenge
items: Slow image loading. The image setup was holding back load times on an image-heavy catalogue.
Merchandising depended on a developer. The theme had no flexible section system, so routine page changes needed code edits.
No structured tracking. The team had no clear view of how customers behaved on the site.

sections.title: My Role
paras: I owned the Shopify theme work: custom Liquid sections with merchant-facing settings, product and collection features, responsive image delivery, the analytics setup and on-page SEO across the catalogue. The merchandising team was the day-to-day user of the section system, so I built it for them to use on their own.

sections.title: What I Built
items: 20+ custom Liquid sections with JSON schema settings, so the team can add, edit and reorder page content in the Shopify editor.
Product experiences and collection filtering built with Liquid, JavaScript and metafields.
Image-loading architecture: responsive sizes, a lazy-loading strategy and separate mobile and desktop images.
Analytics integrations: Google Tag Manager, Google Analytics, Meta Pixel and Microsoft Clarity.
Structured on-page SEO across the full catalogue.

sections.title: Key Improvements
steps: Responsive sizes
Images are requested at widths that match where they're displayed, instead of one large file for every screen.
Lazy-loading strategy
Images further down the page wait until they're needed, so they don't compete with the main image for bandwidth.
Mobile and desktop image pickers
Separate images for mobile and desktop, so phones aren't sent desktop artwork.

sections.title: The Hard Part
paras: Speed and flexibility pull in opposite directions. A section system that lets anyone place any image anywhere can quietly undo performance work. So I treated the image setup and the section system as one problem: the mobile and desktop image pickers live in the section settings, and every page the team builds in the editor keeps the responsive behaviour.

code.note: Simplified sketch of the pattern, not the production code
code.html: {%- comment -%} Banner section: separate art for mobile and desktop {%- endcomment -%} {%- liquid assign desktop = section.settings.image_desktop assign mobile = section.settings.image_mobile | default: desktop -%} <picture> <source media="(max-width: 749px)" srcset="{{ mobile | image_url: width: 750 }}"> {{ desktop | image_url: width: 1600 | image_tag: widths: '800, 1200, 1600', sizes: '100vw' }} </picture> {% schema %} { "name": "Banner", "settings": [ { "type": "image_picker", "id": "image_desktop", "label": "Desktop image" }, { "type": "image_picker", "id": "image_mobile", "label": "Mobile image" } ] } {% endschema %}

sections.title: Business Impact
paras: Improving landing-page performance reduces friction for paid and organic visitors and can decrease abandonment before users engage with the store.
The section system paid off differently. The merchandising team could ship page changes without waiting for a developer, and the analytics setup showed them how customers actually used the site.

sections.title: Results
items: 20+ sections the team edits and reorders in the Shopify editor, without code changes.
Responsive image delivery across an image-heavy catalogue, including the 500+ products I managed.
Analytics through Google Tag Manager, Google Analytics, Meta Pixel and Microsoft Clarity.
Consistent on-page SEO across the catalogue.

diviniti.takeaway: Performance work lasts longer when it's built into the tools the team uses every day. Because the responsive image behaviour lives inside the sections, pages the team builds later keep it without a developer checking each one.

glance.problem: Merchandising depended on a developer, images loaded slowly and tracking was unstructured, across the 500+ products I managed.

facts: Complete build: design, development, SEO and deployment

metrics.label: Tools listed on the current homepage
Original how-to guides alongside the tools

sections.title: Overview
sections.lead: A utility site where trust matters as much as features.
paras: People use tools like these with personal documents: photos for application forms, signed PDFs, scanned pages. FreeToolsHub keeps all of that on the visitor's device. I built the app, the tools, the content and the SEO, and deployed it on Cloudflare with its own domain.

sections.title: The Challenge
items: Private by design. Uploading a passport photo or a signed form to an unknown server is a real risk, so no file could leave the device.
Heavy work in a browser tab. Text recognition, PDF editing, HEIC decoding and background removal run on the client, so CPU-heavy processing must not block the main interface.
A growing catalogue without repeating the work. Each tool needs its own page, instructions, FAQs and metadata, and they all have to stay consistent.

sections.title: Constraints
items: Zero running cost. No paid APIs or databases, so the site is a static export hosted on Cloudflare.
Honest content only. No invented reviews, ratings or statistics, and the privacy policy has to describe what the site really does.
Consent first. Analytics and ads stay off until the visitor accepts and real IDs exist, and third-party scripts load only after consent.
Nothing the visitor types is executed. User-supplied HTML, CSS and code is treated as text, never rendered or run.

sections.title: My Role
paras: I designed and built it end to end: the Next.js app, every tool component and the shared PDF and image logic, the brand and layout, the blog, technical SEO and the Cloudflare deployment.

sections.title: What I Built
items: 93 tools listed on the current homepage: the catalogue spans PDF, image, calculator, developer, text and SEO utilities. The homepage screenshot shows the current count.
A registry-driven site. One typed entry per tool drives its page, metadata, FAQs, related links and search, and content tests fail the build if titles, descriptions or links are wrong.
Technical SEO. Metadata, canonical URLs, Open Graph, JSON-LD and an XML sitemap, plus a post-build check that fails on overlong or duplicate titles and descriptions.
20+ original how-to guides that sit next to the tools and link into them.
Consent-gated analytics. Google Analytics loads only after the visitor accepts, and records which tool was used, never file names or contents.

sections.title: How a File Is Handled
steps: Choose a file
The browser reads the file straight from the visitor's device. Nothing is sent anywhere.
Process on the device
The tool's code loads on demand and runs locally. Heavy work, such as text recognition, runs in a Web Worker so the page stays responsive.
Download the result
The result is built in memory and saved from the browser. The site never holds a copy.

sections.title: The Hard Part
paras: Heavy engines without a heavy site. Text recognition, HEIC decoding and background removal depend on large WebAssembly engines. Shipping them with every page would slow down someone who just wants a word counter. So each tool is its own lazy-loaded chunk, and the heavy engines load only when that tool is used, from the site's own origin instead of a CDN. A build script copies them out of the npm packages, so nothing third-party is fetched at runtime.
The other trap was stale results: if someone swaps the file mid-read, the old run must not overwrite the new one. Each run carries a token, and the worker is terminated as soon as it finishes.

code.note: Simplified from the text recognition tool, not the full component
code.html: // The OCR engine (WebAssembly) loads only when someone presses "Read text" const { createWorker } = await import("tesseract.js"); // Engine and language data come from the site itself, not a third-party CDN const worker = await createWorker(language, 1, { workerPath: `${origin}/ocr/worker.min.js`, corePath: `${origin}/ocr/core`, langPath: `${origin}/ocr/lang`, }); // Runs in a Web Worker, so the page stays responsive const result = await worker.recognize(canvas); await worker.terminate();

sections.title: Results
items: 93 tools listed on the homepage screenshot captured on 23 November 2026.
No uploads. Processing happens on the device, and the site has no backend or database.
Hosted on Cloudflare, with its own domain and security headers.
Checks before every release: typecheck, lint, unit and content tests, and the SEO check all run in one command.

freetoolshub.takeaway: Constraints shaped the design. Ruling out a backend removed storage, accounts and privacy risk in one decision and pushed the effort into careful client-side engineering. The same approach carries over to storefronts: ship less JavaScript and load heavy features only when a visitor asks for them.

glance.problem: People use everyday tools with personal documents, and uploading them to an unknown server is a real risk.
glance.contribution: I designed and built the platform, its browser-based tools, content and SEO; the current homepage lists 93 tools.
glance.outcome: OCR is delegated to a Web Worker rather than the main UI thread, allowing the page to continue handling user interactions while recognition runs.

sections.title: Overview
sections.lead: A complete publishing product, not just a news homepage.
paras: The platform combines a fast, SEO-focused public website with a full admin dashboard. Visitors can browse categories, articles, authors, tags and search, while staff manage content and publishing operations through a protected newsroom.

sections.title: The Challenge
items: One connected editorial workflow. Articles, authors, categories, media, redirects and publishing schedules need to work together instead of living in disconnected tools.
Public performance and private administration. Public pages should be cacheable, while admin pages and mutations must remain authenticated and permission-checked.
Publishing needs more than a text editor. A newsroom also needs structured metadata, media handling, scheduled releases, feeds, redirects and operational logs.

sections.title: My Role
paras: I built the platform end to end: the Next.js application, public page system, admin dashboard, Supabase data and authentication integration, publishing workflows, technical SEO, security layers, automated tests and Vercel deployment.

sections.title: What I Built
items: Public news website: homepage, category pages, article pages, author profiles, tags, search, policy pages, RSS feeds and XML sitemaps.

Admin newsroom: article management with a Tiptap editor, categories, authors, media library, advertising settings, redirects, editorial calendar, scheduled publishing, logs, subscribers and site settings.
Publishing workflows: scheduled publishing, RSS feed imports and connected editorial automation endpoints for content review and operational checks.
Technical SEO: page metadata, canonical URLs, Open Graph and Twitter cards, JSON-LD structured data, XML and Google News sitemaps, robots rules, redirects and noindex handling.

Security: Supabase authentication, writer/editor/admin roles, PostgreSQL Row Level Security, Zod validation, server-side HTML sanitisation, verified media uploads, rate limits and protected cron endpoints.

sections.title: Architecture and Performance
paras: The application uses the Next.js App Router with Supabase for PostgreSQL, authentication and file storage. Public pages use a cookie-less anonymous Supabase client so they can be statically rendered and cached with incremental static regeneration.

Admin actions use authenticated server-side access, check staff roles and rely on database Row Level Security for a second permission boundary. Mutations revalidate affected public paths so editorial changes appear without waiting for the full cache interval.
steps: Public request
Public pages query published content through the anonymous client and use a five-minute ISR revalidation window.
Editorial action
Staff sign in to the admin dashboard; server actions validate input and check the required role.
Database enforcement
Supabase Row Level Security enforces access rules again at the database layer.
Publish and refresh
Scheduled publishing records the release and revalidates public pages so the latest content is available.

sections.title: Quality and Reliability
items: TypeScript type checks and ESLint run as part of the project validation workflow.
Unit tests and database tests cover application logic, migrations and access-control behaviour.
Browser and accessibility checks cover key admin, publishing, SEO, responsive and public-site flows.
Uploads are checked by file content and re-encoded before being stored; article HTML is sanitised before saving.

sections.title: Results
items: One newsroom: public publishing and the editorial admin are connected through a single application.
Editorial operations: articles, media, authors, categories, redirects and publishing schedules are managed from the dashboard.
Search-ready foundations: structured metadata, canonical URLs, sitemaps, RSS and schema markup are built into the platform.
Layered access control: authenticated roles, server-side checks and database-level RLS protect staff operations.

newsmedia.takeaway: The key engineering decision was separating public read paths from authenticated editorial actions. That keeps public pages cacheable while admin operations remain protected by server-side role checks and database-level policies.

glance.problem: Editorial teams need one place to manage articles, media and scheduled releases while keeping staff actions permission-controlled.
